title: Four proposed bets
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four People Ops leads have written their closing one-pager. All four use the word "bet."

**One of them is describing a migration.** Find it, and notice that being a migration isn't the same as being wrong.

artifacts.label: Bet A
artifacts.body: "Change: extend the service-desk assistant from carryover-balance questions to the full leave topic set. Baseline: 412 leave contacts a week, median 6.2 hours to first response, 11% repeat-contact rate, all from saved queries. 90-day measure: repeat-contact rate on leave topics, meaningful move is below 8%. Funding line: we stop producing the monthly manual service report nobody reads — 6 hours a month. Reinvestment: those hours plus the deflected volume go to Priya's document-governance work, specifically retiring the duplicate leave policies. Comes off: the 2019 leave-balance intranet page and its two stale copies. Review: 12 November, Priya holds it. If the repeat rate rises we revert to carryover-only, which we've rehearsed."

artifacts.label: Bet B
artifacts.body: "Change: replace the manual onboarding checklist with the HCM's new agentic onboarding workflow. Baseline: onboarding takes 3.5 hours of coordinator time per hire. 90-day measure: coordinator hours per hire. Funding line: none needed, the agent is included in our existing licence. Reinvestment: coordinators move to higher-value employee experience work. Comes off: nothing yet. Review: end of Q1. Contract is signed, go-live is 6 October and it's in the all-hands deck, onboarding training for managers is built, and the coordinators have been told. We're confident this is the right call."

artifacts.label: Bet C
artifacts.body: "Change: turn off the internal-mobility ranking feature. Baseline: 240 internal applications a quarter, no evidence the ranking improved shortlist quality, and Dana has declined 4 of 31 shortlists: an 87% acceptance rate, which by Module 7's test means it isn't a recommend tier. 90-day measure: internal application volume and hiring-manager satisfaction, to check we haven't made things worse by removing it. Funding line: n/a. This frees Dana's review time. Reinvestment: Dana's hours go to the exclusion list work from Module 6. Comes off: the feature itself, and the review step that existed only to supervise it. Review: 30 days, and we can re-enable in one config change if volume drops."

artifacts.label: Bet D
artifacts.body: "Change: enable the HCM's AI-assisted performance-review drafting for all 3,100 employees. Baseline: managers currently spend an estimated 90 minutes per review; we'll survey after launch to confirm. 90-day measure: manager satisfaction with the review process, and adoption rate, target 70% of managers using it. Funding line: we stop the manual review-quality audit HR does each cycle. Reinvestment: the HRBP team gets that time back for calibration support. Comes off: the review-quality audit. Review: after the cycle completes in March."

reasoning:
**B is a migration, and the last three sentences are how you know.** Contract signed, date in the all-hands deck, manager training built, coordinators told. Apply the test: **is there a state of the world in which you do not proceed?** There isn't. Every remaining decision is about execution.

And note that this isn't a criticism of the plan: onboarding automation may be exactly right, and migrations are legitimate and necessary. The failure is calling it a bet, because that word implies a decision that could go either way, and a function that uses it for things that can't gradually loses the ability to stop anything. Three other tells: **no funding line** ("included in our existing licence" is a licensing fact, not a funding line, coordinator hours still cost money); **"coordinators move to higher-value employee experience work"**, which is the sentence Lesson 1 says means nobody has decided; and **nothing comes off**, which is the fourth term left blank.

**A is the reference answer**, and its strength is the boring parts. Baseline from saved queries with a stated repeat rate. A 90-day measure that would move only if things genuinely improved — **repeat contact detects a wrong answer**, where adoption wouldn't. A funding line naming a specific activity and its hours. A reinvestment commitment naming a **person and a task** somebody could check in six months. Something coming off. And a rehearsed reversion.

**C is the strongest bet on the page and most people do not pick it as a bet at all**, because it looks like housekeeping. It is the fourth term used properly: **turning something off, with a measure designed to catch the possibility that removal made things worse.** Notice what it does with Module 7 — an 87% acceptance rate means the recommend tier was nominal, so the review step existed only to supervise a feature that wasn't earning it, and both come off together. It reduces the surface Modules 3 through 7 have to govern, it frees a named person's time, and it is reversible in one configuration change. If you sorted C as the migration because it lacks a conventional funding line, re-read the test: there is very much a state of the world in which they don't proceed.

**D is the interesting failure, because it has all four terms filled in and still does not work.** The baseline is **"an estimated 90 minutes, we'll survey after launch to confirm"**, which is Module 2's unrecoverable error: a baseline taken after enablement is a measurement of the new state. The 90-day measures are **satisfaction and adoption**, both activity metrics that move whether or not review quality improved. And the funding line is the worst thing on the page: it pays for AI-assisted review drafting by **cancelling the audit that would detect AI-assisted review drafting going wrong.** That isn't a funding line, it is removing the smoke detector to pay for the candles.

The transferable question for your own page: **which of your four terms is doing real work, and which one is a sentence you wrote because the template had a slot?**
